claim: IL-2 and IL-4 are both pleiotropic cytokines and members of a family in which γC (CD132) is a shared receptor subunit.
source: IL-2 and IL-4 are both pleiotropic cytokines and members of a family in which γC (CD132) is a shared receptor subunit.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cytokine receptor families.

claim: IL-2 signals optimize effector and memory T cell responses as a part of normal immune protection.
source: IL-2 signals optimize effector and memory T cell responses as a part of normal immune protection (Boyman and Sprent, 2012; Boyman et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-2 can drive the proliferation of activated CD4+ and CD8+ effector T cells.
source: From a pro-inflammatory perspective, IL-2 can drive the proliferation of activated CD4+ and CD8+ effector T cells (Morgan et al., 1976; Liao et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-2 enhances natural killer cell cytotoxicity.
source: IL-2 can drive the proliferation of activated CD4+ and CD8+ effector T cells (Morgan et al., 1976; Liao et al., 2013), enhance natural killer cell cytotoxicity (Henney et al., 1981; Siegel et al., 1987)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-2 augments B cell proliferation and antibody secretion.
source: IL-2 can drive the proliferation of activated CD4+ and CD8+ effector T cells (Morgan et al., 1976; Liao et al., 2013), enhance natural killer cell cytotoxicity (Henney et al., 1981; Siegel et al., 1987), and augment B cell proliferation and antibody secretion (Mingari et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-2 drives Fas-mediated activation-induced cell death.
source: However, IL-2 is also potently anti-inflammatory, driving Fas-mediated activation-induced cell death (Refaeli et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-2 promotes Treg survival.
source: However, IL-2 is also potently anti-inflammatory, driving Fas-mediated activation-induced cell death (Refaeli et al., 1998) while promoting Treg survival (Chinen et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of IL-2 results in severe autoimmunity and inflammation.
source: However, IL-2 is also potently anti-inflammatory, driving Fas-mediated activation-induced cell death (Refaeli et al., 1998) while promoting Treg survival (Chinen et al., 2016), with its loss resulting in severe autoimmunity and inflammation (Horak, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-2 receptor α (CD25) is a common marker for activated conventional T cells.
source: Its pleiotropy can be partly explained by the strategic and context specific expression of its receptors, with IL-2 receptor α (IL-2Rα; CD25) being a common marker for activated conventional T cells (Tconv) as well as an established constitutive marker for Tregs (Malek, 2008; Spolski et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CD25 is an established constitutive marker for Tregs.
source: Its pleiotropy can be partly explained by the strategic and context specific expression of its receptors, with IL-2 receptor α (IL-2Rα; CD25) being a common marker for activated conventional T cells (Tconv) as well as an established constitutive marker for Tregs (Malek, 2008; Spolski et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CD25 is part of the high affinity IL-2 receptor complex with IL-2Rβ (CD122) and γC.
source: CD25 is part of the high affinity receptor complex with IL-2 receptor β (IL-2Rβ; CD122) and γC, although it can function as a low-affinity receptor in isolation (Waldmann, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CD25 can function as a low-affinity IL-2 receptor in isolation.
source: CD25 is part of the high affinity receptor complex with IL-2 receptor β (IL-2Rβ; CD122) and γC, although it can function as a low-affinity receptor in isolation (Waldmann, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: An intermediate affinity IL-2 receptor excluding CD25 consists of a heterodimer of IL-2Rβ and IL-2Rγ.
source: An intermediate affinity IL-2R excluding CD25 is also known, and it consists of a heterodimer of IL-2Rβ and IL-2Rγ (Boyman and Sprent, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The activity of IL-2 is dependent upon JAK/STAT signaling, with STAT3 and STAT5 being the primary mediators of its transcriptional regulation.
source: The activity of IL-2 is dependent upon JAK/STAT signaling, with STAT3 and STAT5 being the primary mediators of its transcriptional regulation of target genes (Johnston et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The type I IL-4 receptor is comprised of IL-4Rα (CD124) and γC.
source: IL-4 has perhaps an even broader impact and has two receptor forms. The type I IL-4 receptor is comprised of IL-4 receptor α (IL-4Rα; CD124) and γC, whereas the type II receptor contains IL-4Rα and IL-13 receptor α1 (IL-13Rα; CD213A1) (Nelms et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The type II IL-4 receptor contains IL-4Rα and IL-13Rα1 (CD213A1).
source: IL-4 has perhaps an even broader impact and has two receptor forms. The type I IL-4 receptor is comprised of IL-4 receptor α (IL-4Rα; CD124) and γC, whereas the type II receptor contains IL-4Rα and IL-13 receptor α1 (IL-13Rα; CD213A1) (Nelms et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-4 signaling is mediated by the JAK/STAT pathway, with STAT6 being a main transcriptional mediator.
source: Like many cytokines, signaling is mediated by the JAK/STAT pathway, with STAT6 being a main transcriptional mediator (Hou et al., 1994; Gadani et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-4 is historically associated with allergy through its ability to stimulate class switching to IgE and expression of the IgE receptor.
source: IL-4 is historically associated with allergy through its ability to stimulate class switching to IgE and expression of the IgE receptor (Geha et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-4 is critical for parasite clearance.
source: IL-4 is historically associated with allergy through its ability to stimulate class switching to IgE and expression of the IgE receptor (Geha et al., 2003), although it is also critical for parasite clearance (Urban et al., 1991)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-4 is critical for differentiation of naïve T cells into a type two helper (Th2) phenotype.
source: IL-4 is historically associated with allergy through its ability to stimulate class switching to IgE and expression of the IgE receptor (Geha et al., 2003), although it is also critical for parasite clearance (Urban et al., 1991) and differentiation of naïve T cells into a type two helper (Th2) phenotype (Paul, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-4 is a key differentiating factor for wound healing macrophages.
source: Yet, IL-4 is also a key differentiating factor for wound healing macrophages (Gordon, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-4 is known to oppose IL-17-mediated inflammatory diseases like psoriasis and experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE).
source: Yet, IL-4 is also a key differentiating factor for wound healing macrophages (Gordon, 2003), which is essential for tissue repair, and is known to oppose IL-17-mediated inflammatory diseases like psoriasis and experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) (Vogelgesang et al., 2010; Weigert et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-4R signaling has been shown to inhibit neutrophil effector functions in vivo.
source: Furthermore, IL-4R signaling has been shown to inhibit neutrophil effector functions in vivo, which pertains to inflammatory diseases where significant neutrophil infiltrates are found (Woytschak et al., 2016; Impellizzieri et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-4 has been shown to elicit IL-10 in both macrophages and T cells.
source: In fact, IL-4 has been shown to elicit IL-10 in both macrophages and T cells (Krzyszczyk et al., 2018; Mitchell et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IL-2 stimulation drives the expression of IL-4Rα, thereby enhancing subsequent responses to IL-4 through serial activation of STAT5 and STAT6.
source: For example, IL-2 stimulation drives the expression of IL-4Rα, thereby enhancing subsequent responses to IL-4 through serial activation of STAT5 and STAT6, respectively, ultimately leading to Th2 T cell differentiation (Zhu et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tregs cultured with combinatorial IL-2 and IL-4 stimulation resulted in synergistically higher numbers of IL-10 expressing cells compared to single cytokine stimulation.
source: We found that Tregs cultured with combinatorial cytokine stimulation resulted in synergistically higher numbers of IL-10 expressing cells (Figure 1A–C) and IL-10 secretion (Figure 1D) compared to single cytokine stimulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: Tregs cultured with combinatorial IL-2 and IL-4 stimulation resulted in synergistically higher IL-10 secretion compared to single cytokine stimulation.
source: We found that Tregs cultured with combinatorial cytokine stimulation resulted in synergistically higher numbers of IL-10 expressing cells (Figure 1A–C) and IL-10 secretion (Figure 1D) compared to single cytokine stimulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: IL-10 expression as measured by GFP median fluorescence intensity (MFI) was equivalent between IL-2 and IL-2 with IL-4 in IL-10+ cells.
source: However, analysis of IL-10+ cells revealed that IL-10 expression as measured by GFP median fluorescence intensity (MFI) was equivalent between IL-2 and IL-2 with IL-4 (Figure 1E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The synergy between IL-2 and IL-4 in inducing IL-10 production is sex-independent.
source: The sex-independent (Figure 1F) and TCR-stimulation-dependent synergy (Figure 1A–D) was present in FoxP3+ Tregs but not FoxP3- Tconv (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The synergy between IL-2 and IL-4 in inducing IL-10 production is TCR-stimulation-dependent.
source: The sex-independent (Figure 1F) and TCR-stimulation-dependent synergy (Figure 1A–D) was present in FoxP3+ Tregs but not FoxP3- Tconv (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: The synergy between IL-2 and IL-4 in inducing IL-10 production was present in FoxP3+ Tregs but not FoxP3- Tconv.
source: The sex-independent (Figure 1F) and TCR-stimulation-dependent synergy (Figure 1A–D) was present in FoxP3+ Tregs but not FoxP3- Tconv (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: No loss of FoxP3 expression was observed in Tregs cultured with IL-2 and IL-4.
source: The sex-independent (Figure 1F) and TCR-stimulation-dependent synergy (Figure 1A–D) was present in FoxP3+ Tregs but not FoxP3- Tconv (Figure 1A), and no loss of FoxP3 expression was observed (Figure 1G)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Both IL-2 and IL-4 must be present in culture together to manifest the synergistic IL-10 response.
source: We found that both IL-2 and IL-4 must be present in culture together to manifest the synergistic IL-10 response (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: No cytokine or chemokine other than IL-10 was both synergistically and robustly increased by combined IL-2 and IL-4.
source: Remarkably, no cytokine or chemokine other than IL-10 was both synergistically and robustly increased (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) by combined IL-2 and IL-4, including the Treg-associated TGF-β family members (Tran, 2012; Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 1I.

claim: Neither IL-2 nor IL-4 induced autocrine production of the reciprocal cytokine.
source: Moreover, neither IL-2 nor IL-4 induced autocrine production of the reciprocal cytokine (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The combination of IL-2 and IL-4 induces IL-10 expression in FoxP3+IL-10- cells.
source: We observed robust induction of IL-10 expression in FoxP3+IL-10- cells and maintenance of IL-10 expression in FoxP3+IL-10+ cells, with no detectable change in FoxP3 (Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The combination of IL-2 and IL-4 maintains IL-10 expression in FoxP3+IL-10+ cells.
source: We observed robust induction of IL-10 expression in FoxP3+IL-10- cells and maintenance of IL-10 expression in FoxP3+IL-10+ cells, with no detectable change in FoxP3 (Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Nearly every Treg converts to IL-10+ by day 7 of culture with IL-2 and IL-4.
source: To assess this effect beyond 3 days, we cultured Tregs and analyzed them on days 3–7 and found a profound daily increase in the overall percentage of IL-10+ Tregs, ultimately leading to nearly every Treg converting to IL-10+ by day 7 (Figure 1L and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Tregs cultured with combined IL-2 and IL-4 were more proliferative than those cultured with single cytokines or no cytokines.
source: Tregs cultured with the combined cytokines were more proliferative, as measured by the number and magnitude of cell division peaks (Figure 2A, for gating strategy, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), proliferation index, and division index (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Cytokine supplementation led to each subsequent generation of Tregs expressing more IL-10 than the previous generation.
source: We found that cytokine supplementation led to each subsequent generation of Tregs expressing more IL-10 than the previous generation (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Originally IL-10- Tregs that gained IL-10 expression adopted a higher division index than the Tregs which remained IL-10-.
source: Furthermore, staining IL-10- and IL-10+ Tregs with CellTrace prior to culturing and Sytox viability dye after culturing revealed that originally IL-10- Tregs that gained IL-10 expression adopted a higher division index than the Tregs which remained IL-10- (Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Tregs that were IL-10+ on day 0 and remained IL-10+ after 3 days of culture had the highest division index and percentage of the overall population that divided.
source: Furthermore, staining IL-10- and IL-10+ Tregs with CellTrace prior to culturing and Sytox viability dye after culturing revealed that originally IL-10- Tregs that gained IL-10 expression adopted a higher division index than the Tregs which remained IL-10- (Figure 2D), and Tregs that were IL-10+ on day 0 and remained IL-10+ after 3 days of culture had the highest division index and percentage of the overall population that divided.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: IL-10+ Tregs that lost IL-10 expression had a drastic decrease in proliferation.
source: Lastly, the IL-10+ Tregs that lost IL-10 expression had a drastic decrease in proliferation as measured by division index and percentage of cells that underwent division, indicating that IL-10+ Tregs only lose IL-10 expression when they become quiescent and non-dividing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: IL-10-expressing Tregs were significantly more proliferative than Tregs that do not express IL-10.
source: We then compared the division and proliferation indices of IL-10+ with IL-10- Tregs and found that IL-10-expressing Tregs were indeed significantly more proliferative than Tregs that do not express IL-10 (Figure 2E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: IL-10+ Tregs supplemented with combined IL-2 and IL-4 proliferated the most of all conditions.
source: We then compared the division and proliferation indices of IL-10+ with IL-10- Tregs and found that IL-10-expressing Tregs were indeed significantly more proliferative than Tregs that do not express IL-10 (Figure 2E), and that IL-10+ Tregs supplemented with combined IL-2 and IL-4 proliferated the most of all.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The IL-2/IL-4 enhancement of Treg proliferation was lost in FoxP3 conditional knockout of IL-10 (IL-10 cKO) mice.
source: Using a FoxP3 conditional knockout of IL-10 (IL-10 cKO) created by crossing Foxp3cre-YFP (Rubtsov et al., 2008) and Il10fl/fl (Roers et al., 2004) mice, the IL-2/IL-4 enhancement of Treg proliferation was indeed lost (Figure 2G)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: IL-10 autocrine signaling may help drive IL-2/IL-4-enhanced Treg proliferation.
source: Using a FoxP3 conditional knockout of IL-10 (IL-10 cKO) created by crossing Foxp3cre-YFP (Rubtsov et al., 2008) and Il10fl/fl (Roers et al., 2004) mice, the IL-2/IL-4 enhancement of Treg proliferation was indeed lost (Figure 2G), suggesting that IL-10 autocrine signaling may help drive IL-2/IL-4-enhanced Treg proliferation.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing loss of proliferation in IL-10 cKO mice.

claim: Combined IL-2 and IL-4 synergistically increased the number of total Tregs and IL-10+ Tregs over 12-fold in 5 days.
source: Finally, a time course study revealed that of purified Tregs cultured in the presence of all cytokine combinations for 3–7 days, combined IL-2 and IL-4 synergistically increased the number of total Tregs and IL-10+ Tregs over 12-fold in 5 days (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Tregs stimulated with IL-4 alone had impaired suppression activity despite IL-4-mediated increase in IL-10.
source: Treg suppression activity was impaired upon IL-4 stimulation, despite the IL-4-mediated increase in IL-10 (Figure 1), while supplementation with either IL-2 or both cytokines substantially increased Tconv inhibition (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Supplementation with either IL-2 or both IL-2 and IL-4 substantially increased Treg-mediated Tconv inhibition.
source: Treg suppression activity was impaired upon IL-4 stimulation, despite the IL-4-mediated increase in IL-10 (Figure 1), while supplementation with either IL-2 or both cytokines substantially increased Tconv inhibition (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Stimulation by combined IL-2 and IL-4 led to increased IL-10 release by Tregs.
source: Stimulation by combined IL-2 and IL-4 led to increased IL-10 release by Tregs (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Stimulation by combined IL-2 and IL-4 led to significant suppression of IL-4 and IL-17A production by Tconv cells.
source: Stimulation by combined IL-2 and IL-4 led to increased IL-10 release by Tregs (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1A) and significant suppression of IL-4 and IL-17A production by Tconv cells (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cytokine-stimulated IL-10-/- Tregs failed to suppress the proliferation of WT Tconv cells.
source: Next, to assess the role of IL-10 in Tconv inhibition, we repeated the experiment using Tregs isolated from Il10-deficient (IL-10-/-) mice and found that cytokine-stimulated IL-10-/- Tregs failed to suppress the proliferation of WT Tconv cells (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: IL-10-/- Tregs failed to reduce Tconv cytokine expression.
source: Next, to assess the role of IL-10 in Tconv inhibition, we repeated the experiment using Tregs isolated from Il10-deficient (IL-10-/-) mice and found that cytokine-stimulated IL-10-/- Tregs failed to suppress the proliferation of WT Tconv cells (Figure 3D), did not express IL-10 (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 1B), and failed to reduce Tconv cytokine expression (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Treg-specific IL-10 cKO cells failed to inhibit WT Tconv proliferation and cytokine production.
source: Likewise, Treg-specific IL-10 cKO cells also failed to inhibit WT Tconv proliferation and cytokine production, due to a lack of IL-10 release (Figure 3G–I, Figure 3—source data 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: Tregs stimulated with both IL-2 and IL-4 for 7 days showed significantly greater suppression of Tconv proliferation compared to single cytokine conditions.
source: However, Tregs stimulated with both cytokines showed significantly greater suppression of Tconv proliferation (Figure 3J), produced higher concentrations of IL-10 (Figure 3K), and suppressed the production of IL-4 and IL-17A by Tconv cells to a greater degree (Figure 3L) compared to single cytokine conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J-L.

claim: By day 9 of a 1:8 Treg-Tconv co-culture, WT Tregs previously stimulated with both IL-2 and IL-4 overtook greater than 80% of the co-culture.
source: Indeed, we found that by day 9 of a 1:8 Treg-Tconv co-culture, the WT Tregs previously stimulated with both IL-2 and IL-4 overtook greater than 80% of the co-culture whereas IL-10-deficient Tregs from IL-10 cKO mice did not (Figure 3M).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: IL-10-deficient Tregs from IL-10 cKO mice did not overtake the Treg-Tconv co-culture by day 9.
source: Indeed, we found that by day 9 of a 1:8 Treg-Tconv co-culture, the WT Tregs previously stimulated with both IL-2 and IL-4 overtook greater than 80% of the co-culture whereas IL-10-deficient Tregs from IL-10 cKO mice did not (Figure 3M).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: STAT3 phosphorylation was not altered as a result of combined cytokine stimulation in TCR-activated Tregs.
source: While STAT3 is associated with both IL-2 and IL-4, we found that STAT3 phosphorylation was not altered as a result of combined cytokine stimulation in TCR-activated Tregs, although a small amount of STAT3 phosphorylation occurred at 60 min with combined cytokines without TCR stimulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: IL-2 induced low levels of STAT6 phosphorylation in TCR-activated Tregs.
source: IL-2 induced low levels of STAT6 phosphorylation, while IL-4 induced robust STAT6 phosphorylation in TCR-activated Tregs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: IL-4 induced robust STAT6 phosphorylation in TCR-activated Tregs.
source: IL-2 induced low levels of STAT6 phosphorylation, while IL-4 induced robust STAT6 phosphorylation in TCR-activated Tregs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: The addition of IL-2 to the IL-4 and TCR signals resulted in the reversal of IL-4-dependent STAT6 activation.
source: Remarkably, the addition of IL-2 to the IL-4 and TCR signals resulted in the reversal of IL-4-dependent STAT6 activation (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: STAT5 phosphorylation was weak downstream of either IL-2 or IL-4 independently at the concentrations used.
source: We also found that STAT5 phosphorylation was weak downstream of either independent cytokine at the concentrations used herein (Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: IL-2 and IL-4 in combination led to a dramatic and synergistic increase in STAT5 phosphorylation.
source: In combination, however, IL-2 and IL-4 at low concentrations led to a dramatic and synergistic increase in STAT5 phosphorylation, suggesting that STAT5 may be necessary for the synergistic IL-10 and proliferative response in Tregs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: Blockade of STAT5 activity inhibited the IL-2/IL-4 response by over 80% in a dose-dependent fashion.
source: Blockade of STAT5 activity inhibited the response by over 80% in a dose-dependent fashion, as measured by inhibition of IL-10 induction as a percent (Figure 4D) and number (Figure 4E) of IL-10+ Tregs, overall Treg viability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), IL-10 expression on a cellular level (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), proliferation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E), and IL-10 release (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-F.

claim: At high STAT5i concentration, IL-2/IL-4 synergy was lost.
source: Although STAT5i inhibited IL-10 expression and reduced the number of IL-10+ Tregs under all conditions (Figure 4F and G), we discovered that at high STAT5i concentration, IL-2/IL-4 synergy was lost, as illustrated by a lack of difference between the sum of the individual IL-2 and IL-4 responses (Figure 4F and G; stacked bars) and stimulation with both cytokines simultaneously (Figure 4F and G; purple bars).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: STAT5 was necessary to induce the synergistic response characteristic of the IL-2 and IL-4 combination.
source: These data demonstrated that the signaling downstream of individual cytokine receptors was altered by the combinatorial integration of other cytokine-stimulated signals, as was clear for STAT5 and STAT6 activation. Moreover, not only was IL-10 production and Treg proliferation paired events, but STAT5 was necessary to induce the synergistic response characteristic of the IL-2 and IL-4 combination.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing loss of synergy with STAT5 inhibition.

claim: The receptor expression pattern of TCR-activated Tregs without cytokines, with IL-2 or IL-4 individually, and both cytokines were all divergent and distinct.
source: Surface expression was first visualized using principle component analysis (PCA), which demonstrated that the receptor expression pattern of TCR-activated Tregs without cytokines, with IL-2 or IL-4 individually, and both cytokines were all divergent and distinct (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between IL-10 and IL-2Rα (CD25) expression.
source: Further analyses of the data revealed a strong positive correlation between IL-10 and IL-2Rα (CD25) expression (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is a strong negative correlation between IL-10 and IL-2Rβ expression.
source: We also discovered a strong negative correlation between IL-10 and IL-2Rβ expression (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: IL-13Rα1 expression showed a strong positive correlation with IL-10 following combined cytokine stimulation.
source: Curiously, IL-13Rα1 expression showed a strong positive correlation with IL-10 (Figure 5F), similar to IL-2Rα (Figure 5B), following combined cytokine stimulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Supplementation of Treg cultures with recombinant IL-13 in any combination with IL-2 and IL-4 did not impact IL-10 production.
source: Supplementation of Treg cultures with recombinant IL-13 in any combination with IL-2 and IL-4 did not impact IL-10 production (Figure 5G and H)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: The synergistic response to IL-2 and IL-4 is specific for IL-4 and not IL-13.
source: Supplementation of Treg cultures with recombinant IL-13 in any combination with IL-2 and IL-4 did not impact IL-10 production (Figure 5G and H), suggesting that the response is specific for IL-4.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing no effect of IL-13.

claim: Blocking the IL-10R via neutralizing antibody resulted in a profound loss of IL-10 expression downstream of IL-2/IL-4 on a per-cell basis.
source: In order to determine whether IL-10-IL-10R autocrine signaling may also be playing a role in synergistic IL-10 production (Figure 1), we blocked the IL-10R via neutralizing antibody at two concentrations. We found a profound loss of IL-10 expression downstream of IL-2/IL-4 on a per-cell basis (Figure 5J)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: IL-10 signaling promoted further IL-10 expression in Tregs stimulated with IL-2 and IL-4.
source: These findings indicate that IL-10 signaling promoted further IL-10 expression in Tregs stimulated with IL-2 and IL-4, but only played a minor role in their proliferation.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing loss of IL-10 expression with IL-10R blockade.

claim: IL-10 signaling only played a minor role in Treg proliferation.
source: These findings indicate that IL-10 signaling promoted further IL-10 expression in Tregs stimulated with IL-2 and IL-4, but only played a minor role in their proliferation.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing modest decrease in proliferation with IL-10R blockade.

claim: A 1:1 ratio of IL-2/IL-4 was sufficient to suppress HDM-induced asthma-like disease in mice.
source: We found that a 1:1 ratio of IL-2/IL-4 was sufficient to suppress disease, as indicated by reduced bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cell differentials (Figure 6A) and greatly improved lung histology (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Individual cytokines administered at the same doses failed to significantly suppress HDM-induced infiltration or tissue pathology.
source: In comparison, individual cytokines administered at the same doses failed to significantly suppress infiltration (Figure 6A) or tissue pathology (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Mice administered combined IL-2 and IL-4 accumulated more IL-10+ and total Tregs per gram of tissue in lung and spleen.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of lung and spleen cells showed that the mice administered combined cytokines accumulated more IL-10+ and total Tregs per gram of tissue (Figure 6C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: IL-2/IL-4 failed to reduce disease morbidity in IL-10 cKO mice.
source: Unlike in WT mice in both Th1-skewed C57Bl/6 and Th2-skewed BALB/c backgrounds, IL-2/IL-4 failed to reduce disease morbidity in IL-10 cKO mice (C57Bl/6 background), as measured by BAL cell differentials (Figure 6D), H and E tissue histology of infiltrating cells and bronchial epithelial cell hyperplasia (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), and PAS staining of mucus production (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Mucus production was increased in IL-2/IL-4-treated asthmatic IL-10 cKO mice.
source: In fact, mucus production was increased in IL-2/IL-4-treated asthmatic IL-10 cKO mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Mice pretreated with IL-2/IL-4 were significantly protected from developing HDM-induced airway disease.
source: We found that mice pretreated with IL-2/IL-4 were significantly protected from developing airway disease as quantified by BAL differentials and tissue pathology (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: IL-10-deficient mice were not protected from HDM-induced airway disease by IL-2/IL-4 pretreatment and showed increased severity of disease overall.
source: We found that mice pretreated with IL-2/IL-4 were significantly protected from developing airway disease as quantified by BAL differentials and tissue pathology (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), but that mice deficient in IL-10 were not protected and showed increased severity of disease overall (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Mice treated with combined IL-2 and IL-4 had significantly lower lung resistance upon methacholine challenge in a chronic asthma model.
source: Since this model results in tissue remodeling and hyper-responsiveness to bronchial restricting agents, we examined the lung function of the mice using a Flexivent ventilator, and observed that the mice treated with the combined cytokines had significantly lower lung resistance upon methacholine challenge (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: IL-2/IL-4 treatment reduced cellular infiltration, epithelial hyperplasia, mucus production, and tissue remodeling in chronic asthma.
source: Moreover, lung histology revealed reduced cellular infiltration and epithelial hyperplasia by H and E staining, decreased mucus production (PAS staining), and prevention of long-term tissue remodeling (TriChrome staining) when provided IL-2 and IL-4 combination therapy (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: A 1:1 ratio of IL-2/IL-4 was sufficient to suppress EAE disease.
source: We found that a 1:1 ratio of IL-2/IL-4 was sufficient to suppress disease, as indicated by reduced clinical score (out of 5) (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), as well as reduced demyelination and cellular infiltration on spinal cord histology (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Individual cytokines administered at the same doses failed to suppress EAE disease.
source: In comparison, individual cytokines administered at the same doses failed to suppress disease.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: All three delivery schedules (preventative, concomitant, and therapeutic) of IL-2/IL-4 generated significant reductions in EAE clinical score.
source: All three delivery schedules (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A), including preventative (i.e. prophylactic), concomitant (i.e. at the first sign of disease), and therapeutic (i.e. approaching peak disease), generated significant reductions in clinical score (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: IL-2/IL-4 treatment led to significantly reduced MOG-specific Tconv cells in EAE.
source: Flow cytometry further revealed that the cytokines led to significantly reduced MOG-specific Tconv cells (Figure 7D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: IL-2/IL-4 treatment decreased IL-17 within neuronal tissues in EAE.
source: Flow cytometry further revealed that the cytokines led to significantly reduced MOG-specific Tconv cells (Figure 7D) while ELISA showed decreased IL-17 within neuronal tissues (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: IL-2 and IL-4 in combination increased the percentage of CNS and splenic IL-10+ Tregs in MOG-challenged animals.
source: We found that IL-2 and IL-4 in combination increased the percentage of CNS and splenic IL-10+ Tregs in MOG-challenged animals (Figure 7F and G) in correlation with reduced disease.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: IL-2/IL-4 treatment did not increase IL-10 among CNS-localized Tconv cells in MOG-challenged mice.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe increases in IL-10 among CNS-localized Tconv cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A.

claim: IL-2/IL-4 treatment did not increase IL-10 in F4/80+ macrophages in MOG-challenged mice.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe increases in IL-10 among CNS-localized Tconv cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A) or F4/80+ macrophages in MOG-challenged mice with cytokine therapy (Figure 7H) despite IL-4 being a classical M2-polarizing cytokine in macrophages (Loke et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Cytokine efficacy in EAE was lost in both germline IL-10-/- and Treg-specific IL-10 cKO mice.
source: Finally, we found that cytokine efficacy in EAE was lost in both germline IL-10-/- and Treg-specific IL-10 cKO mice, as measured by disease score (Figure 7I–K, Figure 7—figure supplement 3B), cellular infiltration and demyelination (Figure 7J, Figure 7—figure supplement 3B and C), and IL-17A levels in the CNS (Figure 7L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I-L.

claim: The combinatorial signaling mediated by IL-2 and IL-4 in TCR-activated Tregs produced a response divergent from the sum of the two pathways in isolation.
source: In this study, we discovered that the combinatorial signaling mediated by IL-2 and IL-4 in TCR-activated Tregs produced a response characterized by IL-10 expression synergy, selective proliferation of IL-10+ Tregs, differential STAT5 and STAT6 signaling, and distinct cell surface receptor phenotype compared to either cytokine in isolation.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Disease suppression by IL-2/IL-4 was abrogated in mice deficient in IL-10, both globally and conditionally in FoxP3+ Tregs.
source: Disease suppression was paired with increased Treg prevalence and IL-10 expression in Tregs, a reduction in MOG-specific effector T cells in EAE, and was abrogated in mice deficient in IL-10, both globally and conditionally in FoxP3+ Tregs.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: The combinatorial cytokine signaling in Tregs is integrated to generate a unique biological outcome that is divergent from the sum of each pathway in isolation.
source: Together, our data reveal that the combinatorial cytokine signaling in Tregs is integrated to generate a unique biological outcome that is divergent from the sum of each pathway in isolation and robustly enhances and maintains the suppressive ability of FoxP3+ Tregs in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Summary and interpretation of experimental findings.

claim: The dosing of IL-2 and IL-4 used in this study was substantially lower than previous reports showing efficacy for EAE suppression.
source: Although IL-2 and IL-4 have independently shown efficacy in suppressing EAE (Rouse et al., 2013; Racke et al., 1994), the dosing used in this paper was substantially lower. For example, IL-2 limited EAE severity using an i.v. treatment regimen of 10,000 IU/dose, three times per day, for 3 days, totaling to 90,000 IU over the course of the trial (Rouse et al., 2013). Here, we use a total of 2500 IU of IL-2 over the course of the trial as a therapy.
evidence: Comparison with prior literature and experimental data from this study.

claim: At the low doses used in this study, IL-2 and IL-4 alone were ineffective at suppressing EAE disease.
source: At the low doses used in the present study, IL-2 and IL-4 alone were ineffective at suppressing disease (Figure 7A and B); however, when administered together, the cytokine combination significantly suppressed disease.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Bacteroides fragilis is native to a healthy human gut.
source: For example, Bacteroides fragilis, which is native to a healthy human gut (Wexler and Goodman, 2017; Troy, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bacteroides fragilis is known to regulate the peripheral immune system.
source: For example, Bacteroides fragilis, which is native to a healthy human gut (Wexler and Goodman, 2017; Troy, 2010), is known to regulate the peripheral immune system (Johnson et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2015a; Ochoa-Repáraz et al., 2010; Tzianabos et al., 1994)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PSA-specific effector T cells require communication with Tregs.
source: It is now clear that PSA-specific effector T cells require communication with Tregs, and that immune suppression and inflammatory disease reversal depends upon both IL-4 (33, 45) and IL-2 (67)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cytokine therapies have been limited in part due to the short half-life in circulation.
source: From a translational perspective, cytokine therapies have been limited in part due to the short half-life in circulation (Donohue and Rosenberg, 1983; Conlon et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Autologous Treg transfer therapies have been limited by poor expansion and survival of Tregs ex vivo.
source: As such, our findings suggest that IL-2- and IL-4-induced combinatorial signaling may be best harnessed for autologous Treg transfer therapies, which itself has been limited by poor expansion and survival of Tregs ex vivo (Tang and Bluestone, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tregs that underwent stimulation by both IL-2 and IL-4 together retained their activated and IL-10-producing state and exponentially expanded and survived for almost 2 weeks in culture.
source: Here, Tregs that underwent stimulation by both IL-2 and IL-4 together not only retained their activated and IL-10-producing state, but also exponentially expanded and survived for almost 2 weeks in culture with 3 days of cytokine stimulation and 9 days of co-culture with Tconv cells (Figure 3M).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M.
